title: The Concept of Emergency Care and Resuscitation

blocks.text: The Concept of Emergency Care and Resuscitation

Emergency care and resuscitation involve rapid assessment and early intervention. The approach to Emergency care and resuscitation needs to be systematic; hence the use of the ABCs. The ABCs approach provides the framework for evaluation and treatment of severely ill patients.

blocks.text: Primary survey
Airway
Assess the airway to establish patency of the airway. This includes: Looking for signs of airway obstruction (signs of trauma, swelling, secretions, presence of foreign body).
Listening for abnormal sounds like a stridor and snoring.

If there are signs of airway obstruction, intervene by positioning, opening and clearing the airway. Perform a chin lift or jaw thrust maneuver to open the airway (If suspecting cervical spine injury, use the jaw thrust maneuver). Use suction to remove secretions. Airway adjuncts, such as oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway can be used.

blocks.text: Note
Remember to reassess the airway after performing interventions.
Some patient may require use of advance airway devices like endotracheal intubation or surgical airway.
Use video laryngoscopy over direct laryngoscopy helps to improve first-pass success.
emergency intubation
Breathing

Upon completing airway assessment and intervention, assess for the presence of breathing, signs of respiratory distress such as tachypnea, hypoxia, cyanosis, apnea and abnormal breath sounds. Provide oxygen when oxygen saturation is below 92% or when the patient is dyspneic. Oxygen can be administered using the nasal prong, simple face mask, non-rebreather mask or Ambu bag. Advanced interventions include mechanical ventilation.

blocks.text: Circulation

Check for pulse (central pulse) for not more than 10 seconds. If absent, start CPR (Refer cardiopulmonary resuscitation section 1.3). Assess for signs of poor peripheral perfusion (shock) such as cold extremities, prolonged capillary refill, dry mucous membrane and hypotension. If there are signs of shock, establish two (2) IV large bore cannula and give IV fluids (crystalloids) bolus (2lts in adults and 20mls/kg in pediatrics). Limit fluids to individuals whom you suspect of having heart failure, renal failure or malnourished children.

blocks.text: Disability

This involves a rapid assessment of neurological status. This includes assessment for the level of consciousness (use of AVPU or Glascow coma scale), signs of convulsions, random blood glucose level, examination of the pupils and presence of focal neurological deficit. Interventions that can be performed during the disability assessment include correction of hypoglycemia, airway protection, stopping the convulsions by administering anticonvulsant.

blocks.text: Exposure
This involves fully exposing the patient and rapid assessment of the body for signs of trauma, rashes or infection.
Secondary survey

After assessment and stabilization of ABCs during the primary survey, focus is turned into secondary survey. The secondary survey is a systematic assessment of the rest of the body to identify injuries and illnesses. Common approaches include a head-to-toe or organ –system-based assessment. It is important to note that the secondary survey is performed after the primary assessment and interventions.

blocks.text: When performing a secondary survey, if the patient condition changes, then you must stop immediately and redo the primary survey and necessary interventions.
Note:
All patients with compromised airway, breathing, circulation or disability must be attended in the resuscitation rooms. (Refer Triage overview section)
